title: Charged with grandeur (Hopkins, 1877)
hookLine: the world is charged with the grandeur of God
tomorrow: Jesus showed his tears and his anger. what did he keep hidden?

cards: Shake a sheet of kitchen foil in the sun. It doesn't glow evenly. It flashes: here, then there, then everywhere at once.

Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest and a poet, put that flash into a short poem, to answer a question anyone can ask on a dull afternoon: is the world just worn-out stuff, or is something shining through it?

teach.b: Hopkins answers in his first line: "The world is charged with the grandeur of God." Charged, full and ready to spark. "It will flame out, like shining from shook foil".
Then he admits the problem: "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod", and you can hear the feet. Everything is worn by trade and toil, and feet in shoes can't feel the soil.
Then the turn: "And for all this, nature is never spent; There lives the dearest freshness deep down things". Why? Because the Holy Ghost broods over the bent world like a bird on a nest.
Now a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.

The Qur'an, in its third surah, says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in night following day, there are signs for people of understanding: people who remember God standing, sitting and lying down, who reflect on creation and say, our Lord, you did not create this in vain.
One to tell a friend: the Arabic word for those signs, ayat, is also the word for the Qur'an's own verses. Both look at an ordinary sky and won't call it ordinary. And one honest difference.

Hopkins ends with the Holy Ghost, for Catholics one person of the Trinity. Muslims read the signs as pointing to the one God, and Islam does not speak of God as a Trinity. The same sunrise, two names for what's behind it.

how: Some Catholics read Hopkins's God's Grandeur slowly outdoors, as a way of seeing ordinary creation as charged with God; Muslims reflecting on creation sometimes recite the closing verses of the Qur'an's third surah.

o: billed for a grand, costly new church
full of God's greatness, ready to flash out
accused of trying to be as great as God

games.q: the world, charged — tap the pairs.
p: signs in creation, in the Qur'an

s: Hopkins says the world has worn out its wonder
worn on top, yes, but nature is never spent; freshness lives deep down.
the Qur'an calls things in creation signs for people who reflect
the heavens, the earth, night following day: signs for people of understanding.
sharing a wonder means two traditions believe the same thing
they share the wonder; Hopkins names the Holy Ghost, Muslims the one God, without a Trinity.

games.q: a Muslim classmate says the night sky is full of ayat, signs. you've just read Hopkins. what's the honest thing to say back?
o: we both refuse to call the sky ordinary, and we name what's behind it differently.
so we believe exactly the same thing; the names don't really matter.
Hopkins's poem is just about nature, so it has nothing to do with signs.
games.why: the Qur'an calls creation signs for people who reflect; Hopkins calls it charged with God's grandeur. a real shared wonder, and an honest difference: the Holy Ghost for Hopkins, the one God for Muslims.

practice: Pick up the most ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a key, your own hand, and look at it as if it might flash. Find one thing about it you've never noticed before.
If you pray, let the first line come quietly: the world is charged with the grandeur of God.

wordCard.voice: Charged with grandeur. Hopkins's phrase for a world full of God's greatness, ready to flash out. Today's word.

carryVoice: Keep this: charged with grandeur, worn on top and still the dearest freshness deep down. Day done.
